speaking.text: Rubber was a curiosity for a century before it became useful. Untreated, it turned brittle in cold weather and sticky in heat, so its applications were limited to erasers and waterproofing. Vulcanisation, the addition of sulphur under heat, produced a material stable across ordinary temperatures and made the pneumatic tyre possible.

Peat bogs accumulate at roughly a millimetre a year, so a metre of peat represents a thousand years of growth. Because the waterlogged conditions prevent decay, the layers preserve pollen, ash and occasionally human remains in sequence, making a bog one of the most detailed environmental archives available to us.

Public clocks preceded personal ones by several centuries, and their faces originally carried only an hour hand. A minute hand would have been meaningless, since no mechanism of the period could hold accuracy to a minute over a day, and no ordinary activity required that degree of precision in any case.

Whales descend from land mammals that returned to the sea some fifty million years ago, and their skeletons still record the journey. The bones of a hand remain inside the fin, the nostrils have migrated to the top of the skull, and a few species retain the vestigial remnants of a pelvis attached to nothing at all.

Statistical significance was never intended as a threshold for publication. Its originator described it as a rough guide for deciding which results deserved a second look, and he assumed that anything important would be repeated. Treating a single test as a verdict inverts the purpose of a tool designed to prompt further work.

Barbed wire transformed the American plains faster than any legal instrument could have. Timber for fencing was unavailable across most of the region, so open grazing persisted until a cheap way of enclosing land appeared. Within twenty years of its patent the open range had effectively ceased to exist.

chart.title: Reasons given for choosing a postgraduate course

Departmental reputation is 18 per cent, location 12 and funding only 8, the smallest despite being the factor most often discussed in policy. A strong answer contrasts the two leading motives as nearly equal, groups the three institutional and practical factors, and observes that funding ranks lowest.

chart.title: How a scientific paper reaches publication
chart.summary: Six stages from submission to publication. Note that the editorial screen precedes peer review, so many papers are rejected without ever reaching a reviewer, and that revision sits between the two review stages, making the process a loop rather than a straight line. A strong answer follows the sequence with connecting language, identifies the editorial screen as a filter before review, and points out that the path can return to review after revision.

lecture.transcript: I want to talk about why the metric of gross domestic product survives despite everyone agreeing that it measures the wrong thing. Start with what it is. GDP is the market value of goods and services produced in a country over a period. It was designed in the nineteen thirties, largely by Simon Kuznets, to help governments understand the depression and then to plan wartime production, and for those purposes it was excellent. Kuznets himself warned, in the report that introduced it, that the welfare of a nation could scarcely be inferred from such a measure. The objections are familiar. It counts a car crash as economic activity, because repairs and medical treatment are purchased. It ignores unpaid work entirely, so a country where more childcare is done at home appears poorer than one where the same care is bought. It says nothing about distribution, so an economy in which all growth accrues to a hundred people looks identical to one in which it is shared. And it treats the depletion of a forest as income rather than as the liquidation of an asset. Dozens of alternatives have been proposed, several of them well constructed. Almost none has been adopted. And the reason, I think, is not conspiracy or inertia in the usual sense. It is that GDP is calculated the same way in almost every country, has been for seventy years, and therefore permits comparison across space and time. A better measure that only three countries compute is less useful to a finance minister than a flawed measure that everybody computes. Standardisation, once achieved, is extremely difficult to displace, and that is a lesson that reaches well beyond economics.
key: GDP was designed in the 1930s by Kuznets for depression analysis and wartime planning
Kuznets warned that national welfare could not be inferred from it
it counts destructive activity as output, ignores unpaid work, says nothing about distribution and treats resource depletion as income
many well-constructed alternatives exist but almost none has been adopted

lecture.transcript: Today I want to look at how buildings were made to stand up before anyone could calculate whether they would. Structural engineering as a mathematical discipline is about two hundred years old. Gothic cathedrals are three times that, and they are considerably more daring than most modern buildings in their ratio of height to material. So how was it done? Not by calculation, because the mathematics did not exist. It was done by geometry and by precedent. Master masons worked from proportional rules: if the nave is this wide, the buttress is this fraction of that width, the vault springs at this height. These rules were transmitted within lodges, often as closely guarded property, and they were empirical in the strict sense. They encoded what had stood and what had fallen. And a great deal had fallen. Beauvais cathedral attempted the tallest vault ever built and the choir collapsed twelve years after completion; the tower came down later. What we see surviving is a filtered sample, and the failures are largely invisible to us because a collapsed building tends not to be studied. Now here is the part I want to emphasise. When engineers in the twentieth century finally analysed these structures with modern methods, they found that the proportional rules produce results remarkably close to what the calculations recommend, for the specific case of masonry under compression. The rules were not arbitrary. They were a compressed record of several centuries of trial and error, which is a perfectly respectable form of knowledge, and the only real difference is that it cannot tell you what will happen in a situation nobody has tried.
key: structural engineering as mathematics is only about two centuries old, far younger than Gothic cathedrals

swt.passage: The argument that automation destroys employment has been made in almost identical terms in every industrialising economy for two centuries, and has been wrong about the aggregate every time while being correct about particular people. Mechanised weaving genuinely did eliminate handloom weaving as an occupation, and the weavers who protested were not mistaken about their own prospects; many never worked at their trade again. What did not happen was a permanent reduction in the total demand for labour, because the falling price of cloth increased the quantity purchased, and because the wealth released by cheaper goods was spent on things that had not previously existed. The distinction matters because it determines what policy should address. If aggregate employment is the concern, the historical record is reassuring and intervention is hard to justify. If the concern is the distribution of adjustment costs, the record is alarming, since those costs have consistently fallen on specific occupations, in specific regions, over a period longer than a working life. Retraining programmes have a poor evaluation record precisely because they are designed for the first problem while the people using them are experiencing the second, and a forty-eight-year-old machine operator in a town with one employer is not helped by an accurate observation about the economy as a whole.
key: the claim that automation destroys jobs has been wrong about aggregates and right about individuals

swt.passage: Peer review of grant applications consumes an enormous quantity of researcher time, and several studies have questioned whether it earns it. The core finding is that reviewer agreement is low. When the same proposals are sent to independent panels, the correlation between their rankings is modest, and for applications in the broad middle of the distribution it approaches what would be expected by chance. Panels reliably identify the worst proposals and, less reliably, the strongest few; between those extremes the process is largely allocating by a mechanism nobody would defend if it were described honestly. The time cost is substantial: one analysis estimated that the effort spent preparing applications for a single Australian funding round exceeded the working time the awarded funding would purchase. Proposed alternatives include shortening applications drastically, awarding a baseline sum to every qualified researcher, and explicitly randomising among proposals judged to be above a quality threshold. The last of these attracts the strongest objections and has the best theoretical case, since a lottery among comparable applications at least does not consume months of expert time producing a ranking that a second panel would not reproduce.
key: reviewer agreement on grant applications is low, approaching chance for mid-ranked proposals

essay.prompt: Some governments are considering restricting social media access for children under the age of sixteen. Supporters argue this protects young people during a vulnerable period, while opponents argue it removes an important means of connection and is unlikely to be enforceable. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200-300 words.

reading.passage: Predictive policing systems allocate patrols to areas where crime is forecast, using historical incident data, and they have produced a well-documented feedback problem. The model directs officers to a district; more officers detect more offences, particularly minor ones that would otherwise go unrecorded; those records enter the training data; the model becomes more confident about the district. Nothing about the underlying rate of offending need have changed for the forecast to appear vindicated. The effect is strongest for offences whose recorded frequency depends heavily on enforcement effort, such as drug possession, and weakest for those reported by victims regardless of patrol patterns, such as burglary. Vendors have argued that the problem is a data quality issue that better inputs will resolve. The more careful criticism is that it is structural: any system whose outputs influence the generation of its own future inputs will drift in this way, and the remedy has to be architectural, such as training only on victim-reported categories, rather than a matter of cleaning the data.
reading.q: Which of the following are stated or clearly implied by the passage?
options: Increased patrols can raise recorded offences without any change in actual offending.
The feedback effect is stronger for offences whose recording depends on enforcement effort.
The author accepts the vendors' view that better data will resolve the problem.
Burglary figures are less affected because they depend on victim reporting.
Training on victim-reported categories is offered as a structural remedy.

reading.passage: There is a long tradition of treating the introduction of a new medium as a threat to attention, and the objections repeat with striking fidelity. Socrates argued that writing would destroy memory, since a student who could consult a text would not trouble to internalise it. Early critics of the novel warned that immersive fiction would leave readers unable to attend to real obligations. Radio, television and the telephone each attracted the same complaint in turn. What is interesting is not that the critics were always wrong, because in a limited sense Socrates was right: literate cultures do not train memory as oral ones do. It is that the loss is invariably described as a decline rather than as an exchange, and the capacity gained is invisible to the generation that did not have to acquire it.
reading.q: What is the author's main argument?
options: Complaints about new media describe a genuine loss but overlook the capacities gained in exchange.
Critics of new media have consistently been proven wrong about their effects.
Literate cultures have superior memory training compared with oral cultures.
Each new medium has caused a measurable decline in overall human attention.

reading.passage: Urban tree planting programmes are among the most popular environmental interventions available to a city government, and among the most frequently mismanaged. The planting itself is cheap, photogenic and completed within a single political term. Establishment is neither: a street tree requires watering through several summers, protection from vehicles, and formative pruning, and the failure rate for trees left to fend for themselves exceeds half within five years. Cities that report planting figures without survival figures are therefore reporting an input rather than an outcome, and the two can diverge dramatically. The most effective programmes spend a substantial majority of their budget on the years after planting, which produces far fewer trees announced and considerably more trees standing a decade later.
reading.q: What does the passage identify as the main weakness of tree planting programmes?
options: Budgets and reporting favour planting over the aftercare that determines survival.
Street trees are unsuited to urban conditions and rarely survive regardless of care.
Cities plant species that are inappropriate for their local climate.
Tree planting is too expensive to complete within a single political term.

listening.transcript: I want to spend this session on why big infrastructure projects overrun, because the pattern is so consistent that it demands a systematic explanation rather than a series of individual excuses. The figures are striking. Across several hundred large projects studied internationally, around nine in ten exceed their budget, and the average overrun for rail projects is something like forty-five per cent. Now, the obvious explanation is that estimating is hard and that unforeseen problems occur. That cannot be the whole story, because if estimation error were random the overruns would be roughly symmetrical, with as many projects coming in under budget as over. They are not. The distribution is heavily skewed in one direction, and that asymmetry is the thing requiring explanation. Two accounts compete. The first is psychological: optimism bias, a well-documented tendency to underestimate durations and costs even when a person has been burned before. The second is political, and Bent Flyvbjerg has argued for it forcefully. On this account the underestimation is not an error at all but strategic misrepresentation. A project that is honestly costed does not get approved, because it competes against projects that are dishonestly costed. Selection therefore operates on the forecast rather than on the project, and the winner is systematically the one with the most optimistic numbers. Notice that this predicts something the psychological account does not: overruns should be worse where competition for funding is more intense, and that is broadly what the data show. The proposed remedy is called reference class forecasting. Instead of estimating a project from its own details, you find the distribution of outcomes for similar completed projects and place yours within it. It works, and it is unpopular, because it reliably produces a number that makes the project harder to approve.
key: around nine in ten large projects exceed budget, with rail averaging about forty-five per cent
random estimation error would produce symmetrical overruns, but the distribution is heavily skewed
one explanation is optimism bias, a psychological tendency to underestimate
Flyvbjerg argues for strategic misrepresentation: honest costings do not get approved
selection operates on the forecast, so the most optimistic numbers win, predicting worse overruns where competition is fiercer
reference class forecasting places a project in the distribution of similar completed ones, and is unpopular because it works

listening.transcript: Glass is not, as is frequently claimed, a liquid that flows very [slowly]. The belief rests on medieval church windows being thicker at the bottom, which is usually attributed to centuries of gradual [flow]. The actual explanation is manufacturing: crown glass was spun into discs of uneven [thickness], and glaziers sensibly installed each pane with the heavy edge downward. Calculations show that at room temperature any measurable flow would require a period longer than the age of the [universe]. Glass is properly described as an amorphous [solid].

The common swift spends almost its entire life in the [air]. Instruments fitted to individual birds have shown that some remain aloft continuously for ten [months], landing only to breed. They feed on airborne insects, drink by skimming the surface of water in [flight], and mate on the wing. Sleep appears to occur during long glides at [altitude], usually shortly after dusk. The species has consequently lost most of the capacity to [walk], and a swift grounded on flat ground struggles to launch itself again.

A word about the claim that we only ever see one side of the moon because it does not rotate. The moon does rotate; it simply completes one rotation in exactly the time it takes to orbit the earth, which is what produces the constant face. This is called tidal locking and it is not a coincidence. Tidal forces from the earth deformed the moon slightly, and the friction of that deformation acted as a brake on whatever rotation it originally had, until the two periods matched and the deformation stopped shifting. The same process is operating on the earth, slowing our own rotation by a couple of milliseconds a century, and it is why the day is measurably longer now than it was when the earliest tidal deposits were laid down.
options: The moon does rotate, but its rotation period matches its orbital period because tidal friction gradually braked it into that state, a process now slowly lengthening the earth's day as well.
The moon does not rotate at all, which is the reason a single hemisphere permanently faces the earth and the far side was never observed until the space age.
The moon's rotation and orbit happen to coincide by chance, and astronomers expect the alignment to drift apart over the next few million years.
Tidal forces from the moon have accelerated the earth's rotation over geological time, making the modern day considerably shorter than it once was.

listening.transcript: Something about literature searching that took me far too long to learn. The instinct when you begin a project is to read forwards: find a recent paper, then read the newer things that cite it. That is useful, but the more productive direction early on is backwards. Take the best recent review you can find and work through its reference list, then take the most cited items in that list and work through theirs. Within three or four rounds you will keep arriving at the same twenty papers from different directions, and that convergence is the signal that you have found the core of the field. Reading forwards from a single starting point gives you a branch. Reading backwards from several gives you the trunk, and you cannot judge whether a new paper matters until you know what it is departing from.
listening.q: What does the speaker recommend for early literature searching?
options: Work backwards through reference lists until the same core papers recur.
Begin with the newest publications and read forwards through citations.
Read only recent review articles and avoid older primary sources.
Search using as many different databases as possible before reading anything.

listening.transcript: Archives face a difficulty that grows rather than shrinks with time. Several national collections now hold decades of accessions that no researcher has ever seen. The limiting resource in an archive is therefore not storage but [BEEP].

listening.spoken: Penguins have solid bones, unlike almost all other birds. The lightweight skeleton that makes flight possible is a disadvantage underwater, where buoyancy must be overcome with every stroke. Denser bones allow a penguin to dive with far less effort and the deepest recorded dive by an emperor penguin exceeded five hundred metres The same adaptation appears independently in other diving birds, which is a clear example of convergent evolution.

Fireflies produce light with almost no waste heat, converting close to ninety per cent of the energy involved into visible light. An incandescent bulb manages around five per cent, losing the remainder as warmth The reaction depends on an enzyme called luciferase, which is now used routinely in laboratories as a marker because the light produced is proportional to the quantity of the substance being measured.
